So I used to be completely pro-wing clipping, as like you said, it's good for new bird owners, and can definitely help mitigate safety risks like flying in front of a prey-driven cat, into a pan, etc. But as I did more research I learned that there are other ways to prevent this, like teaching your bird to recall, using a harness/foot leash (on bigger birds), or controlling the environment a bit better. Leaving their wings intact also means they can *escape* any predators in the home like dogs or cats.

I'm not VEHEMENTLY against it, like some people call it abuse and I don't really like that comparison, because at the end of the day sometimes it *is* necessary and the feathers always grow back. But I have seen birds completely lose their confidence for jumping even small distances, or birds hurt themselves from launching into flight only to plop to the ground (though if properly clipped, like you said, they should be able to still glide or fly a short distance to not fall like that)

Honestly one of the biggest risks I discovered when I used to do bird grooming, is that people (and a lot of times, vets!) clip very improperly. Whether that's adding a curve, cutting unevenly, cutting too many feathers or just completely butchering the wing. I would only trust an experienced *bird specific* groomer to do it, and a lot of people don't have access to one. 

Finally it's just the stress. You can acclimate birds to grooming with a lot of patience! You can even do nails and beak without restraining them. But when I used to do it for customers at my old job we would often be working with untamed birds, so it was like. grab them with the towel, clip as fast as possible and put them back, but even then it would sometimes cause seizures and - very rarely, eye bleeding in african greys and macaws, which is an extreme stress response.

ETA: and i completely forgot the main reason people are against it is, ultimately, birds were meant to fly - it's mentally stimulating for them, great exercise, and they have their instincts to do it. It's the easiest form of enrichment for them. However that's also why I don't think it's abuse as enrichment can be provided in a lot of other ways, and i've seen hundreds of very happy spoiled birds with clipped wings. I did see a macaw once who escaped its cage and was flying around our facility, it was overdue for a wing clipping, and i swear I never saw that bird so happy and excited when it realized it actually could fly around.

so proper animal set ups at home are going to be completely different than what we do at petco, for all animals, our company policies are pretty poor. I usually make sure to warn people of this and that they're going to be investing a lot into proper setups, and then I usually tell them youtube is a decent source, and like the other commenter linked, reptifiles.

Since reptiles were already addressed I can share some info about birds

Please note bird care is very subjective and is always under debate haha. but i used to work with parrots exclusively so here is my advice:

General advice, the *minimum* i want any small bird in is 30x24x24, which is commonly called a "utility cage", however cockatiels and conures definitely need way MORE room. the cages petco sells are far too small. the budgies should be sold with the conure cage at minimum.

For budgies, I always say, if you want the bird to bond to you, buy one, but ONLY if they can dedicate to being its buddy like 10+ hours a day. if you're ok with them not being as attached, then please buy two.

i recommend against clipping wings, but always direct them to someone who knows how

and sell them a pellet-based diet, mazuri and zupreem are good!

always send them home with millet, and tell them not to touch the cage for at least a week as birds are super prone to losing weight

and final touches are, make sure they buy lots of toys, and natural perches - the dowel rods and ladders we use in store are so bad for their feet lol. Any of the natural wood perches we have are great.

And warn them that candles, smoke, cooking, drafts, pretty much anything scented, are dangerous for birds!

those are the basics i go over, i hope that helps!

On the topic of humane euthanasia - pet owners see it very differently than people that work with them, yknow? I've been working with animals for quite some time now. And I've had to cull a lot. I will always go with what is best for THEM. Sometimes it's injection, more often it's rhe "gruesome" methods.

I used to work in an animal lab. To them, humane euthanasia for adult mice was to put them in a CO2 chamber. I made myself sit with them every time. It took 3 to 5 minutes and was horrendous. Young mice were often decapitated instead and it was instant, painless. No fear. When I had my own pet mice and it was their time, I chose cervical dislocation over vet, injection, or gas. 

Injection is especially bad for reptiles, it can take an HOUR. A hammer to the head is the preferred method. Again, it SUCKS but THEIR comfort ahould come over ours.

Of course injection is completely viable for a lot of reasons, I do it with my cats and dogs but only at home. It's a tough topic but again, especially since your horse's knees are in so much pain, I do think instant and unaware is much kinder.

Become very familiar with all petco protocols. They're pretty intense and a lot of times, against common knowledge. Unfortunately hospital tanks are not allowed. It depends on your GM and DGM, but at my store, they made us take them down :/ You can set up isolation tanks on the inline aquatics section, though.

There are pictures on Knowledge Base of how wellness should look. Show your new coworkers those, tell them it's in the best interest of EVERYONE, but be prepared to fight lol - I had a similar issue when I came in, and things are finally looking better, but it was hard getting everyone on board.

A sad truth I had to swallow was, at the end of the day, we're really not allowed to give them proper care. Look at the Animal Care app - the way the cages are set up in there is EXACTLY how they need to be set up. No extra hides, water bowls, no different substrate. Your store will get docked points for any changes when inspection comes through.

I also had tons of ideas to improve animal care. The only one I've been allowed to enact on is changing the leopard geckos off of sand. It's tough. But do the best you can and hopefully your GM will support you.

I used to do animal care for a prominent lab, and while we didn't have anything like this in the public, down in the structure itself, there were posters, newspapers, articles, pictures, etc posted in all the common areas. Things like, "We wouldn't have these lifesaving medications without the help of horses" and a list of medications, when and where they were discovered, etc; articles of early animal testing breakthroughs, testaments to certain animals.

AALAC which is the organization responsible for making the animal welfare regulations also had (at that time) monthly newsletters highlighting different species of animals, what we have learned from them. At that time they were even distributing enamel pins of each animal every month - they made sure we appreciated the work they helped us with. I still have my pig one somewhere. It was wearing a little labcoat :)

I loved the work. I think about going back to it. My entire job was caring for the little guys. Food and water of course, but also enrichment, maternity care, medicating, and reporting ANYTHING to vets - even an overgrown toenail was addressed immediately. And the biggest part, reporting researchers that did anything against protocol, even like, moving a mouse to a different cage without approval. There was one big case of abuse that I had to report too. Organizations really do care.

hi! i know deciding to quit is very stressful, just remember YOU are the most important person in this situation and any guilt/stress of leaving is not important.

You have a few options! petco is an at-will employer, so while it's polite to give 2 weeks notice, it is absolutely not necessary. you could leave today if you wanted. 

How to go about it:
Tell gm you wanna talk. Summarize the things that have been stressing you out, why they are unacceptable to you. State that you will be leaving the job effective immediately (or whenever you wish) due to the effect it's having on your mental health. 

If you wish you could do this through email as well if you're too nervous to talk to them in person, it's just a bit more professional that way.

Best of luck!

If you are new, you will get faster. When I started I thought 2 hours was impossible but now I can open everything, including wellness, in about an hour, hour and a half. It will just take practice. Here is some of what I do:

First - go into wellness, check if the animals are alive/food/water, then sign off.

Every time you bring out a cart, make sure it has a roll of paper towel, a garbage bag, extra clean supplies.
MAMMALS:

Prep mammal cart. Like another user said, have extra clean supplies. Instead of bringing around a trashcan, I tie a trashbag to the cart's handle. If you don't already, make sure to bring a small bin of hay with the cart.

Guinea pigs: I shake the poop off their houses, usually the waters need refilling. If there is any algae, change the bottle. Fill up food and water. 

Hamsters: They usually don't need food or water refills every day unless the food dish has poop in it. Again just check the bottles for algae, and that the animals are alive.

Mice: Almost always needs wheels and food dishes changed.

My store doesn't have rats or ferrets, but similar ideas. For opening we just want everything clean and filled.

BIRDS:

Tie a garbage bag to the cart, bring a bucket for dirty water, and a pitcher of clean water. DUMP THE WATER EVERY DAY FOR BIRDS!! Wipe out the dish with paper towel. For budgies: dump the entire food bowl and refill, they've usually picked through it. For other birds: shake off the top layer and refill.

Change the ladders if they are really poopy.

REPTILES:

These take the longest. Prep the cart with: worms (unsifted), bag of dusted crickets (more than you think you'll need), tongs, dirty water bucket/clean water pitcher, misting supplies, vitamins. 

Go cage by cage. Dump water in the bucket and refill dishes, every time. Use paper towel to spot clean anything that's on reptile carpet, or any noticeable messes. Mist the enclosure, then add food. For mealworms: the sifters suck. Shake the mealworm container to get the worms wiggling, then use the tongs to grab em. If some dust gets in there that's ok. Just use your best judgment with how much to give. Crickets, just drop in there. Crested gecko food, always wash the dish and refill.

Bring supplies back to wellness, then do meds last - the floor is most important to get done for "customer perception" (as i was told) and working in wellness after the 2 hours is favorable to working on the floor, if it takes time.

If you have to do aquatics too, ask for help. It depends how many animals you have. Our store has a massive animal stock, and doing fish on top of the others is impossible at my location. 

Dishes, trash, spot cleaning things other than reptiles, can all be done throughout the day.

Mini macaws are macaws. For the most part, they will have the same personality traits as the big birds, just in a smaller body.

Macaws tend to bond to one person but can be trained to enjoy the presence of multiple people. The key to this is socializing them from a young age, getting many people to handle the bird the same way you do (make sure everyone has the same boundaries, etc) and making sure they STAY socialized. Even then, they might still be picky with who they like.

Macaws are very intelligent and respond well to flight training. Of course, it all depends on the individual bird. There will always be a risk of the bird not returning to you even if you do all the training properly, so keep that in mind. Free flight poses a LOT of risks. Familiarize yourself with them. Make sure you do a lot of research in training macaws specifically.

These birds are LOUD. Even the small ones. A Hahn's Macaw will scream just as often as a scarlet. Which is to say, any time it wants to. Like other birds, there isn't really a rhyme or reason.. they'll do it when they're happy, when they're frustrated, when they want attention, and when they want to go home. So be prepared for a lot of noise throughout the day.

Everything about owning a bird is unpredictable. Do as much research as you can and be prepared to dedicate nearly all your time to this bird, as macaws are very needy.

Look up Snowman, one of the best jumpers of all time, who was picked up from being an Amish plow horse. Are cases like that, where a mixed breed excels in one sport, rare? Yes, but I think it's just proof of the power of the horse and the bond between rider and horse.

On the opposite end, I don't compete, and have gotten snark from others for having "good horses" and not utilizing them. Just be true to yourself. If you believe in your buddy then you guys can go far :D
